title: Capstone: feed
summary: Balance write amplification against feed-read latency, including the celebrity case.

parts.rule: For a chronological home feed, choose where to pay the join between authors and followers. Fanout-on-write copies a post reference into follower timelines, making reads cheap but amplifying writes. Fanout-on-read stores posts once and merges followed authors during each read. Use follower distribution, posting rate, active-reader rate, and latency targets to choose push, pull, or a hybrid.
parts.why: There is no universally correct fanout mode. Push wastes work for inactive followers and becomes extreme for celebrity authors; pull makes every feed read gather and merge many sources. A strong design shows the arithmetic, moves asynchronous fanout off the request, and explains when a new post becomes visible.
parts.example: Assume a normal author has 200 followers, a typical reader follows 200 accounts, and one celebrity has 10,000,000 followers. At 1,000 posts per second, pushing every normal post creates about 200,000 timeline inserts per second. Persist each post first, then publish FanoutPost(post_id=42, author_id=9) through a durable queue. Workers read followers in batches and upsert timeline(user_id, created_at, post_id), with a unique key on (user_id, post_id) so retry does not duplicate entries. The API returns after the post and fanout intent are durable, not after all 200 follower rows exist; users may therefore see a short propagation delay. A home-feed read queries one user_id partition ordered by created_at and returns the newest 50 references, then hydrates the posts. Do not push a celebrity post into 10,000,000 timelines. Store it on the author timeline and, when a follower reads, merge recent posts from the few celebrity accounts they follow with their precomputed normal timeline. This hybrid caps celebrity write amplification while keeping the common read cheap. Monitor queue age because a growing backlog is user-visible feed lag. Pure pull may still fit a small product with few followees or infrequent reads; the estimates, not the word “feed,” decide.
parts.use: Use the capstone to connect graph shape, capacity estimates, partition keys, queues, idempotency, and consistency. State the baseline ranking rule, calculate normal and worst-case fanout, and define the visibility delay. Hybrid fanout is useful when follower counts are highly skewed.
parts.refuse: Do not fan out to millions of followers inside the post request. Avoid pure fanout-on-read when every feed load must query hundreds of authors under a tight latency target. A queue without idempotent timeline writes or backlog monitoring is incomplete. Do not add ranking infrastructure until the initial chronological contract and access paths are clear.

body:
Rule. For a chronological home feed, choose where to pay the join between authors and followers. Fanout-on-write copies a post reference into follower timelines, making reads cheap but amplifying writes. Fanout-on-read stores posts once and merges followed authors during each read. Use follower distribution, posting rate, active-reader rate, and latency targets to choose push, pull, or a hybrid.

Why it matters. There is no universally correct fanout mode. Push wastes work for inactive followers and becomes extreme for celebrity authors; pull makes every feed read gather and merge many sources. A strong design shows the arithmetic, moves asynchronous fanout off the request, and explains when a new post becomes visible.

Worked example. Assume a normal author has 200 followers, a typical reader follows 200 accounts, and one celebrity has 10,000,000 followers. At 1,000 posts per second, pushing every normal post creates about 200,000 timeline inserts per second. Persist each post first, then publish FanoutPost(post_id=42, author_id=9) through a durable queue. Workers read followers in batches and upsert timeline(user_id, created_at, post_id), with a unique key on (user_id, post_id) so retry does not duplicate entries. The API returns after the post and fanout intent are durable, not after all 200 follower rows exist; users may therefore see a short propagation delay. A home-feed read queries one user_id partition ordered by created_at and returns the newest 50 references, then hydrates the posts. Do not push a celebrity post into 10,000,000 timelines. Store it on the author timeline and, when a follower reads, merge recent posts from the few celebrity accounts they follow with their precomputed normal timeline. This hybrid caps celebrity write amplification while keeping the common read cheap. Monitor queue age because a growing backlog is user-visible feed lag. Pure pull may still fit a small product with few followees or infrequent reads; the estimates, not the word “feed,” decide.

[[diagram:fanout]]

When to use. Use the capstone to connect graph shape, capacity estimates, partition keys, queues, idempotency, and consistency. State the baseline ranking rule, calculate normal and worst-case fanout, and define the visibility delay. Hybrid fanout is useful when follower counts are highly skewed.

When to refuse. Do not fan out to millions of followers inside the post request. Avoid pure fanout-on-read when every feed load must query hundreds of authors under a tight latency target. A queue without idempotent timeline writes or backlog monitoring is incomplete. Do not add ranking infrastructure until the initial chronological contract and access paths are clear.
